hints: Look carefully at where the dark, thick chromosomes are in the photomicrograph. They are all lined up in a single row across the middle of the cell.

If chromosomes are lined up on the equator, that is metaphase. Ask yourself what happens to the centromere and sister chromatids, and to the nuclear membrane, in the stage that comes immediately after this.
walkthrough:
**Identify the stage in the photo**

Look at the chromosomes. They are condensed, thick and lined up along the equator (metaphase plate) in the centre of the cell. This is the classic picture of metaphase.

In metaphase, sister chromatids are still attached at the centromere and the nuclear membrane has already broken down.

**Work out what the next stage is**

Mitosis runs: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. So the stage after metaphase is anaphase.

In anaphase, spindle fibres shorten and pull sister chromatids apart to opposite poles.

**Apply this to the table**

Two sister chromatids remain attached? In anaphase, no. The centromere divides and chromatids separate to become independent chromosomes.

Nuclear membrane? It broke down in prophase and stays absent through metaphase and anaphase. It only re-forms in telophase. So in anaphase it is still not present. That matches option A.

options.A: Correct. In anaphase, sister chromatids have separated (so no longer attached) and the nuclear membrane is still absent.
options.B: Not correct. Chromatids do separate, but the nuclear membrane does not re-form until telophase, not anaphase.
options.C: Not correct. The nuclear membrane is absent, but sister chromatids do not stay attached in the next stage, they separate in anaphase.
options.D: Not correct. The nuclear membrane already broke down in prophase, so it is not breaking down now, and chromatids separate rather than stay attached.
